title: Love Each Other, and Keep the Door
sum: The Elder writes to "the chosen lady and her children," whom he and all who know the truth love "in truth" (1:1-3). He is glad to have found some of her children walking in truth, and he asks her to keep the command they had from the beginning: love each other. Love, in turn, means walking by God's commands (1:4-6).

Then comes the reason for the letter. Many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh; such a person is "the deceiver and the antichrist" (1:7). The readers must guard what was worked for, and remember that anyone who "goes ahead" and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God (1:8-9). So if a teacher comes without that teaching, they are not to take him into the house or even say "Greetings!" to him, since to welcome him is to share in his work (1:10-11). The Elder has more to say, but hopes to say it in person (1:12-13).
readings: Read this way, "the chosen lady" is a congregation and "her children" are its members; "your chosen sister" is the church where the Elder lives. The letter is then a circular warning from a leader to a church in his care: keep loving each other, and do not open your meeting to teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. The shift between "you" singular and "you" plural, the love of "all who have come to know the truth" for her, and the greeting from a sister who sends no word herself all fit this reading.

Read this way, the Elder writes to a real Christian woman, perhaps a widow, perhaps named Kyria, who leads a household, and perhaps a house church, some of whose children he has met. The warning then lands in a home: the house she opens to traveling teachers is where the false teaching would spread. Plummer, who kept both readings open, thought the change from "you" singular to "you" plural fits a mother and her family as well as a church.

views.H: Christians met in houses and depended on traveling teachers, who depended on hosts. The Didache, an early church manual, shows the same world: receive whoever comes in the Lord's name, then test him, and do not listen to a teacher who teaches "another doctrine" (11.1-2; 12.1). Irenaeus reports that John at Ephesus would not stay in a bathhouse with Cerinthus, who taught that "Christ" came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before he suffered (Against Heresies 3.3.4; 1.26.1).
views.C: The letter names neither its writer nor its readers. Eusebius counted 2 and 3 John among the disputed books, and some in Jerome's day gave them to "John the presbyter" instead of the apostle. Most scholars think one writer produced 2 and 3 John, and that 2 John is closely tied to 1 John (many shared phrases); a minority doubt that one man wrote both, and Rudolf Bultmann held that 2 John was a forgery based on 3 John. Dates proposed run from the 60s to about 110.
views.L: Thirteen verses built on three words: truth (five times), love (four) and command (four). The letter has the shape of an ordinary letter of its day: a greeting, a reason for joy, a request, a warning, the hope of a visit and greetings. Plays on words tie it together: the joy of 1:4 and the forbidden "Greetings!" of 1:10-11 are the same Greek verb.
views.J: The Elder speaks like a Jewish teacher: "walking" for a way of life (the root of halakhah), the command "from the Father," and the fear of a teacher who leads people away from what they first received, as Deuteronomy 13 warned against a prophet who urges Israel off the road God commanded. "Mouth to mouth" (1:12) is a Hebrew idiom: God speaks with Moses "mouth to mouth" (Numbers 12:8).
views.T: The church read 1:10-11 as a rule about heretics. Irenaeus quoted 1:11 as the teaching of John, the Lord's disciple; at Carthage in 256 a bishop quoted 1:10 to argue that those baptized by heretics must be baptized again; Stephen, bishop of Rome, took the other side in that dispute: people coming from a heresy were not to be baptized again. Clement of Alexandria commented on the letter around 200. See the deep dive below.

deep.b:
The Elder says only that they "do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh" (1:7), that they "go ahead" and do not remain in the teaching of Christ (1:9), and that they travel and seek hospitality (1:10). Three answers are given.

Docetists. Many scholars think of teachers who said Jesus only seemed to have a body (from Greek dokeō, "seem"). J. L. Houlden, in his commentary on the letters of John, takes the verse as evidence that such ideas already existed when the letter was written.

Cerinthus and his kind. Irenaeus, writing about 180, describes Cerinthus, a teacher in Asia, who said Jesus was the son of Joseph and Mary, that "Christ descended upon him in the form of a dove" at his baptism, and that "Jesus suffered and rose again, while Christ remained impassible" (Against Heresies 1.26.1). Such a teacher would not deny that a man Jesus lived, but would deny that Jesus Christ, one person, came in the flesh. Irenaeus also tells, from people who heard Polycarp, that John left a bathhouse in Ephesus at once when he saw Cerinthus inside, calling him "the enemy of the truth" (3.3.4).

Those who left 1 John's church. 1 John speaks of antichrists who "went out from us" (1 John 2:19) and of spirits that do not confess Jesus (1 John 4:2-3). 2 John may warn a nearby church about the same people, now traveling. Plummer thought the same persons may be meant in both letters.

deep.h: Closing the door: how 2 John 10-11 has been used
deep.b:
The rule is short: do not take such a teacher "into the house," and do not say "Greetings!" to him (1:10-11). How far it reaches has been argued from the beginning.

The early church. Irenaeus quoted 1:11 as the teaching of John, the Lord's disciple (Against Heresies 1.16.3), and told how Polycarp, meeting Marcion, answered his greeting with "I do know you, the first-born of Satan"; the apostles and their followers, he says, would not even speak with corrupters of the truth (3.3.4). Clement of Alexandria's comment on the letter advises against discussing divine things with such people. At the Council of Carthage in 256, Aurelius of Chullabi argued from 1:10 that if such people may not be received into a house, they may not be admitted into God's house without the church's baptism. That council stood with Cyprian of Carthage. Stephen, bishop of Rome, had ruled the other way: as Cyprian quotes him, "Let nothing be innovated... except what has been handed down"; he "forbade one coming from any heresy to be baptized in the Church," so that such people were received with the laying on of hands for repentance (Cyprian, Letter 73.1-2). The verse was used on one side of a dispute between churches, not by both.

Later practice. The Mennonite Dordrecht Confession (1632, article 17), which teaches shunning, does not cite this letter; it bases the practice on 1 Corinthians 5:9-11 and 2 Thessalonians 3:14, not on this letter, and add that the shunned must still be helped when they are "needy, hungry, thirsty, naked, sick," and admonished "as brethren" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). See the topic page on church discipline.

Cautions. Plummer urged great care before applying the verse: is the case really parallel, is the man really a teacher of unbelief, will severity win him or only win him sympathy? "Let us never forget the way in which the Lord treated Pharisees, publicans and sinners." He read "Greetings!" as covering "any act which might seem to give sanction to the false doctrine or shew sympathy with it."

deep.title: Claude's theory: the same door, shut both ways
deep.b: This is my own reading. In 2 John the Elder tells a house church to shut its door on traveling teachers who do not bring the teaching (1:10). In 3 John, Diotrephes shuts his church's door on the traveling brothers the Elder sends, and throws out those who let them in (3 John 1:9-10). Both letters turn on the same act: whether a church takes in the people who come to it. If the two letters were sent at about the same time, as their matching endings suggest, the Elder may have been fighting with the very tool he recommended: the right of a local church to refuse visitors. That would explain why 3 John stresses testimony (3 John 1:3, 1:6, 1:12): a church can only know whom to receive by trusted witnesses. John Painter argues that 2 John is the letter Diotrephes refused (3 John 1:9), pointing to the overlap between 2 John 9 and the hospitality theme of 3 John; most scholars, C. H. Dodd among them, think the refused letter was a lost letter of recommendation, and Plummer ruled out 1 and 2 John. The irony of the shared tool is my own point.

echoes: 1 John 2:7-8; 1 John 2:18-23; 1 John 4:1-3; 1 John 1:4; 1 John 5:3; John 13:34; John 14:15-17; John 15:4; John 15:12; John 16:24; Mark 13:9; Mark 13:22; 3 John 1:1; 3 John 1:3-4; 3 John 1:13-14; Numbers 12:8; Deuteronomy 13:1-5; 1 Timothy 1:2; Acts 15:23

settings.to: "the chosen lady and her children": a church and its members, or a Christian woman and her household, in tradition in the province of Asia
settings.when: while traveling teachers who did not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh were going from house to house (1:7, 1:10)
settings.why: To open with love and truth, the two things the letter defends. The Elder ties himself and "all who have come to know the truth" to the readers, so that the warning which follows comes from a family, not a stranger. The promise "will be with us" counts the readers in before any warning is given.
views: The lady and her children stand for a congregation and its members (see the note).
A real woman and her family, perhaps named Kyria (see the note).

settings.what: The old command: love each other
settings.to: the lady ("you" singular) and then all her children ("you" plural)
settings.when: after meeting some of her children who were walking in truth
settings.why: To set the ground before the warning: the readers already have what they need, the command they heard at the start. Love is defined as obedience, so no new teacher can offer a "higher" love apart from God's commands. Readers who had heard John 13:34 would hear Jesus' own command.

settings.what: The warning about deceivers, and the rule for the house
settings.to: the readers as a group: the household or house church that received traveling teachers
settings.when: as teachers who "do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh" were going from church to church
settings.why: To stop false teaching from getting a base. The rule binds the hosts of the house where the church met: they are not to give such a teacher lodging or the welcome that would mark him as approved. It applies to a teacher who "comes" without the teaching, not to every stranger, and its purpose is to protect what the readers had received (1:8). Knowing that churches met in homes, and that a teacher lived on his hosts' welcome, explains why the door is the line drawn.
views: "Into the house" means into the church's meeting, where a teacher would be heard.
The rule also covers private hospitality, since a guest teacher lodged with a family.

settings.to: the lady and her children, with greetings from "the children of your chosen sister"
settings.when: as the Elder hopes to travel to them soon
settings.why: To say that a letter is only a stopgap: the full joy comes from meeting "face to face." The greeting from the sister's children, whether a sister church or relatives, reminds the readers that they belong to a wider family of churches.
